Starting a small compost bin at home
A compost bin turns kitchen scraps and garden waste into dark, crumbly soil. You do not need much space: a lidded box about the size of a laundry basket is enough for a small household, and it can sit on a balcony or beside a fence.
Begin with a layer of coarse material such as twigs or torn cardboard so air can move underneath. On top of that, add green material like vegetable peelings, coffee grounds and cut grass, then cover it with brown material like dry leaves or shredded paper. A rough rule is two parts brown to one part green.
What to keep out of the bin
Cooked food, meat and dairy, which attract animals and smell strongly.
Plants with disease, because the pile may not get hot enough to kill it.
Anything treated with strong chemicals, including painted wood.
Moisture matters more than most beginners expect. The contents should feel like a wrung-out sponge: damp, but never dripping. If the pile smells sour, it is too wet, so stir it and add dry leaves. If nothing seems to happen, sprinkle a little water and turn the material over.
How long does it take
In warm weather a well-managed bin can give usable compost in about three months. In a cool season it may take twice as long. You will know it is ready when the original scraps can no longer be recognised and the smell is like forest soil, see the guide to soil for ways to use it.
Patience is the main tool; the bin does the rest while you are busy with other things.
Spread a thin layer around plants in spring, or mix it into pots before sowing. Keep a small bucket in the kitchen so that peelings go straight to the bin, and empty it every two or three days.
